text: A Modest Proposal for Preventing Readers from Being a Burden to Authors, and for Making Them Beneficial to Publishers. A satirical essay arguing for overturning fair use, first sale doctrine, and other copyright precedents to give authors total control, citing specific cases like Folsom v. Marsh, Bobbs-Merrill v. Straus, Baker v. Selden, Feist v. Rural Telephone, Campbell v. Acuff-Rose, and Sony v. Universal, with detailed legal reasoning for each.
label: analysis

text: Mumbo Jumbo by Ishmael Reed - Pulling back the curtain on reality. Written in 1971, as relevant today as it was back then. It's like a Pynchon novel from a black POV, creative formatting and a healthy dash of Assassin's Creed. It's what Kuang's Babel tried to do, but by a competent author. It's a real takedown of colonialism that has real depth, not just a series of stereotypes.
label: analysis

text: Jade Hunter by Charles Mossop (Review). This book tells two stories: a piece of Jade carved into a Ming Dynasty masterpiece and the search for that lost masterpiece. The story remains interesting all the way through. The ending was an unexpected, yet pretty realistic surprise. The historical details never bog down the search.
label: analysis

text: My take on The Starless Sea. The Starless Sea is about what happens when a story loses its organizing logic and becomes deconstructed into just its DNA. I liked the idea but didn't love the execution. Everything felt so shallow and surface level. There were just so many symbols, they can't all be equally important, so they ended up feeling meaningless. I also disliked the repetition of Zachary's name.
label: analysis

text: Has anyone read One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (Solzhenitsyn)? A great depiction of life in a Gulag. This novella focuses on the human experiences in imprisonment rather than Soviet politics. The descriptions of the Siberian cold were particularly potent. The only issue is I wish I could've read this in Russian because the English translation wasn't amazing.
label: analysis

text: The love of my life and I connected in the margins of Stoner by John Williams, and I may never see him again. We bonded over our love of books. I began annotating, writing all my notes in the margins. The relationship between Stoner and Katherine completely took over my reading experience. He never gave the book back to me.
label: reaction

text: In the Shadow of Eight of Collin Gosselin: thoughts and feelings. Just finished this memoir, narrated by Collin himself. It was absolutely devastating. I don't usually cry at books but I cried a couple times. I will no longer be supporting TLC by watching their shows.
label: reaction

text: Shadow of the Wind by Carlos Ruiz Zafon. I'm reading one of the most beautifully written books I've ever read. I read it alongside my dad while we were actually in Barcelona, where the story is set. My father passed away three months ago, and this memory came back to me while rereading it.
label: reaction

text: The curious case of the Table of Contents. Most newer books I've read have something in common: no Table of Contents. Does anyone know why we have gone away from this? Did anyone else enjoy having one?
label: reaction

text: Finally got around to finishing Stephen King's It. I dislike Bill at the end of it. It's obvious Bill is a stand-in for Stephen and he's so pretentious about it. He's the only character who isn't externally flawed, unlike Mike, Bev, Eddie, and Richie. As an adult he cheats on his wife with only a minor bit of reflection.
label: analysis

text: People who DNF or dislike books because they dislike the characters: why? I've never had to like characters to enjoy a story. The only thing a character has to be is well written. Sadie and Sam from Tomorrow, Tomorrow, and Tomorrow were both assholes but very real, believable characters. Marx was a nice guy but a much less well written character.
label: analysis

text: Oh dear. Oh dear oh dear. Daddy Long Legs (1912) by Jean Webster. I realised it was published in 1912, which makes it even less understandable why people loved it in the eighties. We loved the crap out of that awful book when we were teens. Barf. What was wrong with us?
label: reaction

Brunner tackles religion, which runs throughout a big portion of the story. Finally getting a taste of his more new-wavy material.

text: Taipei Story should be called Taipei Diary. R.F. Kuang's new book is not held together by a distinctive plot. It feels more like a fictionalized diary than a novel. None of the topics are fully developed, it lacks a plot, rising tension, resolution, and characters I care about. The author failed to develop her narrator's character properly so the episodes feel choppy like diary entries.
label: analysis

text: Hiding in the Deeps: John Wyndham's Out of the Deeps. It begins with fireballs falling into the oceans, ships disappearing, and creatures attacking. This is complete apocalyptic SF with horror elements, screaming Wells's War of the Worlds but still its own thing. Wyndham takes a slow burn approach that enhances the dread he's going for.
label: analysis

text: Is American Psycho still the American Psycho? Yes. It's insane how relevant a story published in the early 90s as a reaction against consumerist Wall-Street culture is more relevant today than ever. Reading it puts you in direct dialogue with Bateman's inner monologue, his actual headspace, juxtaposed with how everybody around him treats him. That inner monologue is fascinating because it's such a deeply private, personal thing that is both horrifying and humanizing.
label: analysis

text: Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel - tidbits from the book launch. She said it would be interesting to see a character who realizes they devoted their life to the wrong thing. I'm left in awe of the beautiful ending, though I had hoped for more resolution. I thought it was interesting how Nico and Kareem would've been amazing together, but each ended up with the wrong partner, so each kid was taken care of by the better parent from another dimension.
label: analysis

text: What do you do if reading more doesn't make you any better at reading comprehension, though? I don't know how to think deeply about pretty much anything, not good at picking up on symbolism or themes. I needed to have my hand held and be told what to look for before it occurred to me something might be there.
label: reaction

text: The Mill on the Floss and Maggie's Impossible Dilemma. Maggie is chastised again and again by Tom, her brother. The roots of their conflict lie in childhood dynamics, an obvious way to confront the status of women in Eliot's society. Maggie's independent spirit is tested over and over by the male figures in her life. Death is the only way Maggie could escape the trap set for women.
label: analysis

text: Since eyes are on Stockholm this week: to which writer would you award a posthumous Nobel? My nominee would be Tove Jansson, for her psychological depth, her big-heartedness, and the way she embraced difference and otherness. Jansson's books are hymns to nature, friendship, tolerance and the freedom to be oneself.
label: analysis

text: Do you buy books from Barnes & Noble? The books cost near list price both in store and online, not offering savings compared to an independent bookstore. A new hardcover of Yesteryear is $14.99 on Amazon, half the price of the $30 it costs at B&N in store. Is it catering to impulse purchases?
label: analysis

text: Dreaming of Amelia by Jaclyn Moriarty. It's a ghost story told through multiple first person POVs, following two mysterious scholarship students. My favourite thing about her books is how distinct every character's POV feels, they all have their own individual style and personality. The writing style is simple but so effective and feels very realistic.
label: analysis

text: Good Eating: Robert A. Heinlein's Orphans of the Sky. A short fix-up novel of two novellas from the 40s, only about 128 pages. Very much a space opera where existence on a massive spaceship has reduced them to devolve into a feudal state. It's not a really deep book, but it's a quick read that is loads of fun!
label: analysis

text: Just finished The Sun Also Rises by Ernest Hemingway (1926). It must be somewhat autobiographical, as Hemingway served as an ambulance driver in WW1 where he was badly injured. Reading it felt less sophisticated and polished than The Old Man and the Sea, which made sense once I learned it was a very early work, written 25 years earlier.
label: analysis

text: Whistler by Ann Patchett is the best book I've read all year. Oh my god if this wasn't the most beautiful story on reconciliation and family and lost time and love and connection. I absolutely adored this book so much. I haven't read something so heartfelt and warming and tender in a very long time.
label: reaction

text: Only a week until the new Vollmann! The new Vollmann, a table for fortune, drops next week on four volumes and 3k pages. Should get it the day after my birthday, excited! I pre-ordered for $140 a few months ago, it hits at $200 even.
label: reaction

text: Scattered thoughts after finally finishing Middlemarch by George Eliot. Mr. Casaubon is OCD representation to me, his treatment of Dorothea is inexcusable but I couldn't help feeling sorry for him. Lydgate's arc just about broke my heart, that marriage fully crushed his spirit while Rosamond never spares a thought for his feelings. As lovely as the epilogue is, my stomach dropped reading that his hair never became white, he died at 50.
label: analysis

text: Just finished Mistborn: The Final Empire, my first Brandon Sanderson book. The worldbuilding stuff was a bit amateurish to me, not like GRRM does. There was a ton of exposition, helped by the fact the main character is new to everything. With GRRM, when he drops a metaphor, it ties into a thematic element; in Mistborn there doesn't seem to be that amount of care or thought given.
label: analysis

text: Lost Boys Duet | Jessie Walker (10/10). This review might less be a review and more of my thoughts spilled across digital ink. I have read these books over a half a dozen times since it came out. I have cried and felt my heart break right alongside theirs. This book has taught me about life and people and living it in a way that no other story has.
label: reaction
